title: How to View Archived Emails in Gmail (2026 Guide)
summary: Learn how to view archived emails in Gmail on web and mobile, plus search operators, keyboard shortcuts, and tips to recover archived messages fast.
body_text: Archived emails in Gmail can feel like they've vanished, especially when a reply, invoice, or old outreach thread suddenly matters again. The fast answer is that archived mail lives in All Mail , and you can also pull it up with in:archive in Gmail search. Once that clicks, finding, unarchiving, and troubleshooting archived messages becomes a simple workflow instead of a guessing game. Gmail handles archiving differently from most email clients. It removes the Inbox label, but the message still stays searchable and recoverable, which is exactly why power users rely on search more than folder browsing. What Happens When You Archive an Email in Gmail When you archive an email in Gmail, you're not moving it into a separate archive folder. You're removing the Inbox label, and the message stays in All Mail . Google's help page says archived messages live there, and it also gives the direct search shortcut in:archive for finding them quickly ( Google Help on archived mail ). Why that matters in daily use That structure changes how Gmail should be used. A thread can be archived, stay threaded, stay searchable, and still be brought back with Move to Inbox whenever it needs attention again ( Google Help on archived mail retrieval ). For sales teams, recruiters, and founders, that means old conversations don't disappear into a dead folder. Practical rule: archive things you want to keep, delete only what you truly do not need. This is also why many users think archived mail is “missing.” It's not missing, it's just no longer sitting in the Inbox view. In Gmail, the Inbox is a filtered view, not the full mailbox, so archived items remain part of the account and can still be found by sender, subject, keyword, or date. That makes archiving useful for keeping the inbox clean without losing history. It also means you should expect archived mail to behave like any other Gmail content, not like a separate store that needs special recovery. Finding Archived Emails on Desktop Gmail On desktop, the standard path is simple. Open Gmail, expand More in the left sidebar, then click All Mail . Archived messages sit there alongside everything else, and they won't show the Inbox label next to the thread name ( Zapier's Gmail archive guide ). If the mailbox is busy, scrolling isn't the right move. Search is faster. Gmail's own help directs users to All Mail and also supports in:archive for isolating archived messages, which is usually the cleanest way to jump straight to the thread you want ( Google Help on archived mail ). The exact recovery loop Open All Mail from the left sidebar. Search or scan for the message. Open the thread . Click Move to Inbox if you want it visible again. That last step matters because it restores the Inbox label without changing the rest of the conversation history (Google Help on archived mail recovery). If the thread was part of an ongoing conversation, Gmail's threading usually keeps everything together, which is helpful when a client replies weeks later. A lot of people expect an archive bin, then overcomplicate the search. Gmail is easier than that. All Mail is the retrieval view, and in:archive is the faster shortcut when you already know you're looking for something archived. For teams that care about inbox hygiene, this is also why archive is safer than a hard delete. It keeps the thread available for future follow-up, legal record keeping, or reference before a new outreach sequence. If keeping the inbox tidy is also about avoiding needless promotion-tab clutter, a practical companion guide is how to avoid Gmail's promotion tab . Finding Archived Emails on Android and iOS A phone is usually where archived mail gets recovered in a hurry. In Gmail for Android, Google's help says archived messages live under Menu → All mail , and you can also surface them with in:archive ( Google Help for Android ). On iPhone or iPad, open the Mailboxes view and look for All Mail if your account shows that label. The part that trips people up is consistency. Google does not always expose All Mail the same way across personal and Workspace accounts, and some devices tuck the label away or hide it entirely. On mobile, search often beats label browsing because the app's label layout can change from one account to another. A simple recovery flow usually works best. Start with the search bar and enter in:archive if you want only archived messages. If you already remember who sent the email, search by sender name or email address instead. On shared or Workspace accounts, check the account switcher before you spend time hunting through the wrong mailbox. If you open an archived thread and want it back in view, use Move to Inbox from the message actions. Mobile Gmail is fine for quick recovery, but search is usually more dependable than hunting through labels. That matters for outreach teams checking mail between meetings. On a small screen, label navigation can be inconsistent, while search stays direct and predictable. If a shared account shows odd label visibility, switch accounts first before deciding the message is gone. The same approach helps when a filter or forwarding rule seems to hide mail. Search by sender, subject, or in:archive , then narrow from there instead of relying on the sidebar alone. The mobile video walkthrough is here for a visual check, especially if the app layout looks different from the web version. Gmail Search Operators That Surface Archived Mail Search is not a backup plan in Gmail, it's one of the main ways archived mail is meant to be found. The simplest operator is in:archive , which returns archived messages directly and is the cleanest option when you already know the message was archived ( Google Help on archived mail ). The operators worth using in:archive . Use this when you want only archived mail. Example, in:archive invoice . -in:inbox -in:sent -in:draft . Use this when you want messages outside the usual live views. Example, -in:inbox -in:sent -in:draft project update . has:nouserlabels . Use this when labels are messy or missing. Example, has:nouserlabels contract . How-To Geek also notes that negative inbox filters can surface messages that are not in the usual folders, which is useful when Gmail's label state is messy or when a search returns too much mail ( How-To Geek on finding archived emails ). When each search pattern helps If a sender remembers the conversation but not the exact folder, in:archive is the quickest route. If the mailbox has lots of moving parts, the negative filters help isolate mail that is not sitting in Inbox, Sent, or Drafts. If labels are inconsistent, has:nouserlabels is a practical way to surface mail that never picked up a user label in the first place. The best search is the one that matches what is actually broken, not the one that looks clever. A useful habit is to start broad, then narrow. Search the sender name first, then add in:archive if the result set is too noisy. That saves time compared with scrolling through All Mail , especially in high-volume inboxes where old conversations stack up fast. Archive vs Delete and When to Use Each A thread that should stay searchable belongs in Archive . A thread that has no future use belongs in Delete . Gmail treats those actions very differently, so mixing them up can cost you time later when you need to find a conversation fast. Action Recoverable Searchable Storage Best for Archive Yes, in All Mail Yes Remains in the mailbox Threads you want to keep Delete Yes, while in Trash Yes, while in Trash Removed after Trash handling Junk, obvious clutter Archive keeps the message in Gmail, so it still shows up in search and in All Mail . Delete sends the message to Trash, where it can still be recovered for a while, but it is no longer part of your normal working mailbox. That difference matters if you handle client threads, receipts, contracts, or outreach you may need to reopen later. For a side-by-side explanation of how teams usually separate the two actions, see delete email in Gmail and Outlook . Archive is the safer choice for ongoing work. If a thread may come back in a week, a month, or during a handoff, keep it in Gmail and archive it. Delete fits obvious spam, newsletters you never want to see again, and messages with no practical value once you have read them. A simple decision rule Archive if the message is still useful later. Delete if the message is dead weight later. That rule works for most inbox cleanup. It keeps you from deleting a thread that should have stayed searchable in All Mail , and it keeps the mailbox from turning into a pile of conversations you no longer need to see every day. If your team handles both Gmail and Outlook, compare the deletion flow before people start clearing mail by habit. The wrong habit is easy to form, and it usually shows up when someone needs an old thread that was sent to Trash instead of archived. Keyboard Shortcuts and Power-User Habits for Archived Mail A good archive workflow starts with the keyboard. In Gmail, g then a jumps straight to All Mail , so you do not have to keep opening the sidebar just to find an archived thread. If you are cleaning up after replies all day, the archive action itself is faster too, which makes it easier to keep the inbox clear without losing anything you may need later. Habits I use when archived mail matters The fastest pattern is simple. Handle the message, archive it from the inbox right away, then go back to the next item. Use the archive shortcut: archive a thread the moment it is done. Jump to All Mail quickly: press g then a whenever you need the archive view. Keep a saved search: store in:archive if you check archived threads often. Use undo right away: Gmail can reverse an accidental archive immediately after the action. A fast archive habit beats a perfect folder system that nobody follows. I also keep the archive-related view easy to reach when the sidebar gets collapsed a lot. Even a small habit, like pinning or starring the view you open most, cuts down on clicks during a long workday. The goal is not to memorize every Gmail shortcut. The goal is to get from “where did that thread go” to “found it” as quickly as possible. For support teams and outreach teams, that speed matters because archived mail is usually the material that comes back later. A saved search plus a keyboard habit removes a lot of repeated navigation, especially when the inbox keeps moving. If search results feel too broad, tighten them before you start clicking through labels. A query like in:archive paired with a sender or subject line is often faster than browsing by hand, and if hidden archive behavior is part of a wider deliverability problem, a close look at spam confidence level guidance can help you separate visibility issues from inbox placement issues. Troubleshooting Missing Archive and Quick FAQ If All Mail is missing, start by checking whether the label is hidden rather than assuming the message is gone. Gmail's view changes across desktop, Android, and iOS, and Workspace accounts can expose labels differently depending on admin settings and sidebar choices. When search pulls in too many threads, narrow it fast. Add in:archive , then pair it with a sender, subject, or a negative term so you are not scrolling through every related conversation. If you work in a Workspace inbox, confirm you are in the right account first, then check whether a filter, label rule, or forwarding setup is changing what you can see. If a message still feels buried, search the sender name and subject line directly before you keep clicking labels. Gmail search is usually the better tool when archive views differ across devices or when the sidebar is trimmed down. For teams checking reply history or bounce patterns, hidden archived threads are worth finding because they often hold the context you need. A close look at spam confidence level guidance can help separate visibility problems from filtering or inbox placement issues. Quick FAQ Where are archived emails stored in Gmail? They live in All Mail , not in a separate archive folder. Gmail keeps them searchable, so you can find them by sender, subject, keyword, or date. Can archived emails be moved back to the inbox? Yes. Open the message in All Mail or from search, then choose Move to Inbox . Gmail restores the Inbox label right away. Do archived emails count toward storage? Yes, they remain part of the mailbox. Archiving removes inbox clutter, but it does not remove the message from your account. Why does archived mail look different on shared or Workspace accounts? Label visibility can vary by account state, device, and admin settings. If the sidebar looks different, search is usually the most reliable way to find the message. Does Gmail search archived messages automatically? Yes, Gmail search covers archived mail by default. in:archive is just the faster way to isolate only archived threads.

title: From Operational Buyer to Agent Supervisor: The Procurement Workforce of the Future Feb 25, 2026 Read more
summary: Lio (formerly known as askLio) builds the world's first AI procurement workforce for enterprise companies worldwide. Every purchase request is managed by specialized agents working in parallel: researching vendors, negotiating terms, managing approvals, and tracking deliveries simultaneously.
body_text: The Three Layers of Tomorrow’s Procurement Department The real disruption isn’t software. It’s structure. Multi-agent systems introduce a new three-layer model for procurement. 01 At the top sits Strategy Communication Leadership and the CPO define sourcing priorities, risk appetite, supplier strategy, governance standards, and performance objectives. → This layer defines what should happen. 02 Strategy Translation is the new role Agent Supervisors convert strategy into operational logic: negotiation parameters, approval rules, risk thresholds, supplier prioritization, escalation triggers, and compliance frameworks. They design and refine Agent Operating Procedures. They don’t execute tasks; they design the system that executes them. → This layer defines how it should happen. 03 Strategy Execution Here, AI agents operate across systems, tools, and stakeholders. They interpret purchase requests, validate suppliers, match documents, conduct operational negotiations, route approvals, and coordinate directly with ERP systems and other agents. Agent-to-agent communication replaces manual coordination loops. Execution becomes always on, scalable, consistent, and data-native. → This layer ensures it actually happens. Together, these layers form a new enterprise architecture: management defines strategy, procurement translates it into operational logic, and agents execute at scale. The competitive advantage will not be the agent. It will be the buyer behind it. Agents follow logic. Humans define it. Operational buyers once checked data, formatted requests, routed approvals, and reconciled mismatches. Tomorrow, they will design agent logic, supervise performance, manage strategic exceptions, and continuously optimize execution systems. The systems remain. The execution layer changes. Procurement doesn’t disappear. It becomes the strategic brain behind an autonomous execution engine.

title: IceCure: SIO Petitions NCCN to Include Cryoablation in Breast Cancer Treatment Guidelines, Citing IceCure's FDA Clearance of ProSense®
summary: The petition by The Society of Interventional Oncology (SIO) includes adding criteria for patients aged 50-69 who are poor surgical candidates or…...
body_text: The petition by The Society of Interventional Oncology (SIO) includes adding criteria for patients aged 50-69 who are poor surgical candidates or who decline surgery in the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) treatment guidelines, expanding the current eligible population of patients aged 70 and above CAESAREA, Israel , July 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- IceCure Medical Ltd. (Nasdaq: ICCM) ("IceCure," "IceCure Medical" or the "Company"), developer of minimally-invasive cryoablation technology that destroys tumors by freezing as an option to surgical tumor removal, today announced that the Society of Interventional Oncology ("SIO") has submitted a formal petition (the "SIO Petition") to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network ("NCCN") Breast Cancer Guidelines Panel, requesting the inclusion of percutaneous cryoablation without surgical excision as a Category 2B option for carefully selected patients with low-risk, early-stage breast cancer. The SIO Petition specifically proposes adding a Category 2B footnote recommending that percutaneous cryoablation without surgical excision may be considered as an alternative to breast-conserving surgery after shared decision-making, for patients aged 70 years or older with unifocal, ultrasound-visible invasive ductal carcinoma ≤1.5 cm, grade 1–2, hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, and clinically node-negative disease. The SIO Petition further recommends the consideration of patients between the ages of 50-69 who are either poor surgical candidates or decline surgery when cryoablation is combined with whole-breast radiation therapy and endocrine therapy. In support of its recommendation, the SIO Petition cited the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's ("FDA") marketing authorization of IceCure's ProSense® cryoablation system in October 2025. ProSense® is the first and only medical device to receive FDA marketing authorization specifically for the local treatment of biologically low-risk breast cancer in women aged 70 and older with tumors ≤1.5 cm who receive adjuvant endocrine therapy. The recommendation follows the March 2026 update to the American Society of Breast Surgeons (ASBrS) resource guide , which now supports cryoablation for appropriately selected patients with low-risk, early-stage breast cancer. Potential Significance Potential inclusion of cryoablation in the NCCN Breast Cancer Guidelines could increase clinical awareness and support broader consideration of this minimally invasive option for appropriately selected patients. Guideline recognition is often viewed as an important factor in clinical adoption and may influence reimbursement discussions over time. The SIO is a professional organization focused on advancing interventional oncology through education, research, and advocacy. The NCCN is a not-for-profit alliance of leading U.S. cancer centers that develops and publishes the widely used NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology. These guidelines are among the most influential evidence-based recommendations in cancer care and are frequently referenced by clinicians, institutions, and payers. About IceCure Medical IceCure Medical (Nasdaq: ICCM) develops and markets advanced liquid-nitrogen-based cryoablation therapy systems for the destruction of tumors (benign and cancerous) by freezing, with the primary focus areas being breast, kidney, bone and lung cancer. Its minimally invasive technology is a safe and effective option to surgical tumor removal that is easily performed in a relatively short procedure. The Company's flagship ProSense® system is marketed and sold worldwide for the indications cleared and approved to date including in the U.S., Europe, and Asia. title: Big names, big matches and big bets: Flutter’s 2026 World Cup wrapped
summary: An epic World Cup has drawn to a close, after more matches than ever before. We look at the breakout teams and the star players that Flutter’s customers bet on.
body_text: Record-setting performances Despite ultimate disappointment for Argentina, this was Messi's tournament and, given his experience and talent, it's unsurprising that he set new records in 2026. He finishes having played more World Cup matches ( 34 ) than any other player, and broke Ronaldo's record as the oldest player to score a World Cup hat-trick. But he was far from the only player to set records. Ronaldo became the first player to score in six consecutive World Cups, and Spain's goalkeeper finally saw his record run of World Cup games without conceding a goal ended at 650 minutes by Belgium's Charles De Ketelaere . Kane became England's leading World Cup scorer, overtaking Gary Lineker, and Mbappé became the Frenchman with the most World Cup matches (21), surpassing Hugo Lloris . One random stat : the 2026 final was the first since 1978 not to feature a Bayern Munich player. Bigger and better? With 48 teams, this World Cup was always going to deliver more goals and more storylines than any before. And growing rumors suggest that the 2030 tournament, to be hosted in Morocco, Portugal and Spain, with early matches in South America, could be expanded yet again to 64 teams. If so, there will be even more chances for the underdogs to win hearts and for the big stars to break records. And, of course, for Flutter's customers to bet on it all.
